NEW DELHI: A global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted operations across offices as Outlook email, Teams calendars and the tools that connect ChatGPT and Claude to Microsoft's workplace services remained paralysed.The problem, which started late Thursday (India time), was partially restored on Friday evening though intermittent issues persisted. By late evening in India, Microsoft said mailbox access was improving, and delayed emails were being processed, while stating that it had found no indication of a cyberattack. This was the second disruption since Oct 2025 when MS Azure services faced an eight-hour-long global outage.Companies that rely on MS services were forced to opt for other alternatives such as Slack, Webex and Zoom to keep their operations going. Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles cited the outage in a stock exchange filing and shifted its quarterly results webcast with Jaguar Land Rover executives to StreamCart. IBM reportedly moved workplace communication to Slack during the disruption. HDFC Bank told customers on X that its banking services remained available.Airlines and airport operators said operations continued while email communication with passengers was disrupted. Travellers who bought or changed tickets during the outage had to download them from the airline's website or app if their confirmation email did not arrive. Airport operators said they were unable to send emails. Air India rerouted incoming messages, IndiGo directed passengers needing urgent help to its 6E Skai chatbot, and Akasa Air asked customers to call or use social media.Overseas, Australia's sanctions office directed urgent enquiries to the phone. In UK, National Pharmacy Association warned that disruption to NHS email could delay prescriptions. On Thursday, Microsoft first flagged trouble accessing work mailboxes in the Americas. In India, complaints picked up mainly as offices opened on Friday.Outage tracker Downdetector logged around 3,800 Outlook complaints at 10.12am, close to the overnight peak.“We regret the disruption today’s outage has caused for many of our customers,” Puneet Chandok, president of Microsoft India and South Asia, wrote on LinkedIn. “Our global teams continue to work with urgency to resolve the issue.”The problem centred on Exchange Online, the service that runs workplace email and calendars. Some servers unexpectedly went offline, leaving fewer machines to handle the same workload.Some stopped responding again when users reconnected.Microsoft began reversing a recent network change that coincided with the start of the disruption and was investigating whether it triggered the outage. Teams chats and calls could still work even when calendars and meeting invites failed.Anthropic said most email, calendar and search requests through Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector were failing. Some users could not open Claude for Outlook, while others had trouble performing mail and calendar tasks. OpenAI said ChatGPT users could have trouble setting up new connections to Microsoft services and that some existing connections were also failing.Anthropic separately investigated sign-in errors affecting Claude.ai, Claude Code and its developer platform. It began investigating at 3.28pm IST and said at 4.35pm that it had deployed a fix and was monitoring recovery.
Article Summary: Global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted operations across offices as Outlook email, Teams calendars and tools that connect ChatGPT and Claude to Microsoft's workplace services remained paralysed. The problem, which started late Thursday (India time), was partially restored on Friday evening though intermittent issues persisted. Microsoft said mailbox access was improving, and delayed emails were being processed.

Article Title: 'Extraordinary circumstances': US grounds all departing flights over safety concerns
Article Text:
US grounds all departing flights over safety concerns

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop, citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”, after a communications outage affected air traffic control operations across the country.The FAA directed all departing flights to remain grounded until further notice, while inbound international flights would be handled on a case-by-case basis. The agency also warned that equipment outages could lead to airborne holding at airports across the national airspace system.The FAA had earlier announced a ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport due to a communications issue, according to its website.Also Read| US flight chaos: Nearly 500 departures disrupted, thousands stranded as FAA halts take-offs nationwide; what we know so far US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the communications problem had affected all 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft travelling between airports nationwide. FAA technicians were investigating the issue.US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the outage was the result of a deliberate attack.“There is no indication yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us.It's just a telecommunications outage,” Mullin said.“Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying,” he added.Also Read| US flight disruption: Air India flags possible delays to US operations Authorities have not provided a timeline for resuming normal flight operations. Mullin said investigators would also examine whether the outage was linked to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system designed to identify problems and recommend alternative flight routes. However, the system operates from a single location near Washington, DC, and sends recommendations to air traffic control centres.The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a malfunction in a key FAA computer system disrupted flight operations. Before that, a similar nationwide restriction had been imposed following the September 11, 2001, attacks.The disruption has also drawn attention to the ageing technology used by the country's air traffic control system. The government has been working to modernise the infrastructure since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. The overhaul includes replacing miles of ageing copper wires with fibre-optic lines and gradually upgrading radio systems at airports across the country.However, significant work remains. Duffy has said an additional $30 billion would be required to complete the modernisation, with the White House lobbying Congress to approve the funding.
Article Summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered a nationwide ground stop. The FAA directed all departing flights to remain grounded until further notice. Inbound international flights would be handled on a case-by-case basis. The agency warned that equipment outages could lead to airborne holding at airports across the national airspace system.

Article Title: ‘Deer in the headlights’: Colette Kress went from clashing with Huang to leading Nvidia
Article Text:
File photo: Colette Kress appointed Nvidia’s new interim CEO after Jensen Huang’s resignation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nvidia former-CEO Jensen Huang has reported to have previously confronted the new acting CEO and CFO Colette Kress, likening her to “a deer in the headlights”.Huang interrupted Kress during her presentation, according to a person familiar with his remarks cited by The Wall Street Journal. He later called her a “reporting CFO”, suggesting she could report the numbers but was not equipped to help him shape strategy or make decisions.The exchange offered a glimpse into the tensions inside Nvidia as Huang pushed the company deeper into an increasingly risky web of financing arrangements. Kress had been questioning the scale of those commitments, including deals involving companies that were also major buyers of Nvidia chips.Now, following Huang’s departure on Thursday, Kress has been named Nvidia’s interim chief executive, putting her in charge of a company grappling with questions over its AI investments, internal oversight and succession planning.According to Reuters, Kress and her team had clashed with Huang and the company's sales executives over multibillion-dollar financing deals involving OpenAI and AI infrastructure firms such as Lambda.The arrangements were part of Huang's effort to support customers and sustain demand for Nvidia chips, but critics warned that the company risked financing its own customers and creating a circular AI economy.One of the biggest proposals involved an Ohio data-centre project for OpenAI. Nvidia had considered providing a $250-billion financial backstop to help the AI company secure loans for the facility, which was expected to be filled with Nvidia chips. Kress subsequently reworked the proposal, cutting Nvidia's initial commitment to $120 billion, people familiar with the deal told Reuters.The Wall Street Journal reported that Kress had raised questions about how Nvidia should select such deals, value the guarantees and calculate their returns. She also tried to rein in Huang's son-in-law, Nico Caprez, who had been helping arrange financing for cloud providers and data-centre developers.Nvidia eventually paused some of its financing initiatives, with proposals facing closer scrutiny from the executive team and board. Huang also pushed his staff to develop a framework for assessing whether guarantees were worthwhile, including the chip sales they could generate.Kress had publicly defended the strategy even as concerns mounted. In August, she rejected the description of Nvidia's arrangements as circular financing, arguing that they would deliver strong returns.“We recognise the scale of this support, and we know some will call this circular financing. We see it differently,” she said. “The equity returns on our invested capital will be excellent.”Her appointment now places her at the centre of the challenge she had once questioned. Reuters described Kress as a pragmatist who could reassure customers and suppliers during the transition, and potentially adopt a less confrontational approach to Washington than Huang, particularly on export controls.But whether she can preserve the technological ambition and appetite for risk that powered Nvidia's rise remains an open question. Some analysts have questioned whether a finance executive can provide the kind of technology-driven leadership the company needs.Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 after finance roles at Microsoft, Cisco and Texas Instruments. She has spent more than a decade as Huang's CFO, watching the company's valuation soar as its chips became indispensable to the AI industry.In a memo to employees on Thursday, she praised Huang and said she would continue “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.Her appointment comes as Nvidia faces a leadership crisis triggered by revelations about Huang's personal relationships. He stepped down after reports of two extramarital affairs, one involving a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative and another involving an Nvidia employee, according to Reuters.Kress must now take charge of the company as it confronts not only uncertainty over its future leadership and investment strategy, but also the fallout from the circumstances surrounding Huang's exit.
Article Summary: Colette Kress has been named Nvidia’s interim chief executive. She has spent more than a decade as Jensen Huang's CFO. Kress clashed with Huang over multibillion-dollar financing deals involving OpenAI and AI infrastructure firms such as Lambda.

Article Title: Huang's China affair may fix Howard Lutnick, the man who wanted to fix India
Article Text:
Lutnick faces heat over alleged delays in curbing China-linked chip exports, exposing divisions within Trump's cabinet

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, the roadmap for major trade deals was simple: countries like India and Brazil had to be “fixed” to set an example to the world; specifically, PM Modi needed to make a placatory phone call to President Trump; and China needed to be kept dependent on the United States. Except, when it came to selling American AI chips to Beijing, it turns out he was less a hawk and more a dove, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang.Allegations from Lutnick’s own cabinet colleagues that the US commerce department sat on recommendations from other US agencies to sanction China-linked Megaspeed, now accused of spiriting advanced Nvidia AI chips to Beijing via a honeytrap operation, has suddenly put the commerce secretary’s job on the line. In a stunning development on Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly threw Lutnick under the bus, disclosing that the Departments of Treasury, War, USTR, and State were all in favor of putting Megaspeed on the “entity list” for months, “but commerce has the pen. ”"You will have to ask commerce about their internal process...I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s….any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies and gives the Chinese an advantage," Bessent told reporters in more public dissonance in the Trump cabinet.Despite occasionally presenting himself as a China hawk, Lutnick's philosophy when it comes to AI chips was hardly a secret and he had articulated it with characteristic bluntness over months: America, he argued, should sell enough advanced chips to Chinese developers to get them "addicted to the American technology stack." The idea, which was also advanced by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, was to keep the US ahead technologically while ensuring that China continued to use American chips, software, and infrastructure rather than letting it build an entirely independent ecosystem that could eventually challenge US primacy.The problem with Bessent’s dumping on Lutnick though is that President Trump himself previously approved sales of certain Nvidia processors, including H200 chips, to China, broadly reflecting Huang's and Lutnick's argument that America should compete commercially rather than surrender the Chinese market altogether. At the same time, Trump also reportedly authorised crackdowns on suspected chip diversion on three occasions this year, only for implementation to stall, reflecting the conflict between backing the commercial logic of selling chips and the national-security imperative of preventing their diversion.Trump, for his part, has not yet abandoned Lutnick amid growing bipartisan Congressional scrutiny. The White House has declared that the President maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, praising his contribution to America First trade policies, tariffs and manufacturing investments. But the President's own position on China chips is hardly consistent with the tough line being demanded by national-security officials.Beyond the strategic dimension of Washington trying to maintain the technological upper hand, the issue is becoming a political hot potato domestically with Democratic lawmakers, chuffed by the mid-term election verdict, jumping on the issue. Republican Senators are also emboldened by results that have weakened Trump. “This whole thing is an intergalactic freak show….how do they know the chips went to the company (Megapseed) and not to the Communist Party of China?’ asked Louisiana Republican John Kennedy.More fireworks and disclosures are expected ahead of Congressional hearings in the coming weeks. The Republican chairs of three House panels -- Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on China, and Intelligence -- have asked Jensen Huang to sit for a joint, closed-door interview on December 1, followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. Lutnick is also scheduled to appear before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10.The latest developments have dramatically raised the stakes for both Lutnick and Huang amid growing infamy for the Nvidia founder and CEO. Reports of Huang having a third extramarital relationship involving another Nvidia employee emerged on Thursday, even as the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that Huang had privately belittled his successor Colette Kress, describing her as "a deer in the headlights" during a meeting this summer, after she questioned some of his increasingly aggressive investment decisions.Trump, meanwhile, has remained remarkably sympathetic to Huang, even after his departure from Nvidia. In a pre-recorded interview with Stephen Smith aired on Thurday, the President said he had spoken to the embattled icon on Wednesday and that "he's going through hell," while describing him as a "tremendous talent" who would somehow land on his feet.
Article Summary: commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire over alleged delays in curbing China-linked chip exports, exposing divisions within Trump's cabinet. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly threw Lutnik under the bus, disclosing that the Departments of Treasury, War, USTR, and State were all in favor of putting Megaspeed on the “entity list” for months, “but commerce has the pen. ”

Article Title: The out-of-pocket trap: Insurance penetration as the unlock for access
Article Text:
Asia doesn't lack hospitals — it lacks payers. Insurance, not construction, breaks the out-of-pocket trap. (AI-generated image)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Views expressed are personal. Dr. Amit Varma is Co-founder and Managing Partner of Quadria Capital. Abhinav Kejriwal is the founder of PreventiveHealth.AI and a graduate of Stanford Graduate School of Business.

Every few months we are asked the same question in a boardroom somewhere between Mumbai and Ho Chi Minh City - where is the next hospital, the next clinic chain, the next diagnostics platform? It is an incomplete question. Asia does not have a shortage of healthcare supply so much as a shortage of people who can afford to use it.Consider the arithmetic. Across low- and lower-middle-income Asia, households still pay roughly 43 cents of every healthcare dollar directly from their own pockets. In Bangladesh the figure is close to 80 cents. In India, after a decade of public scheme expansion, it hovers near 40. The WHO's South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions carry the highest share of people on Earth facing catastrophic health spending. We have built an industry on the assumption that demand exists. What exists is need. Demand requires the ability to pay, and in most of Asia that ability is absent at precisely the moment it matters.This is the out-of-pocket trap. A family in rural Bihar or Mindanao defers care until the condition is acute, because the cost is theirs alone. Acute care is more expensive and less successful. The bill arrives, and the household sells an asset, borrows at usurious rates, or pulls a child from school.Medicines alone account for more than 60% of out-of-pocket spending in South Asia, and the share is higher still among the poorest fifth. Illness becomes impoverishment, and impoverishment makes the next illness harder to treat. The trap compounds.Providers are caught in it too. A hospital that serves cash-paying patients faces lumpy demand, high receivables risk, and a ceiling on what it can charge before patients simply walk away. It responds by concentrating in cities, favoring elective procedures, and underinvesting in primary and chronic care, which is exactly the care that keeps people out of the emergency ward. Capital follows the same logic. The private hospital in Gurugram or Jakarta is a fine business. The clinic 200 kilometers away is a fine idea. The unlock is not another bed. It is a payer.One of us has spent the better part of two decades financing that supply, so we say this with some discomfort. Every market in Asia that has meaningfully widened access did so by widening who pays, not only who treats. Thailand's Universal Coverage Scheme, launched in 2002, cut catastrophic spending and raised utilization without bankrupting the state. Indonesia's JKN, for all its deficits and delays, now covers more than 270 million people and has changed the shape of private investment across the archipelago. India's Ayushman Bharat extended a hospitalization cover of about US$6,000 to roughly 500 million people, and private hospital chains in tier 2 and tier 3 cities now plan capacity around it. In each case the payer arrived first and the supply followed, at a lower cost of capital and across a wider geography.Insurance does 3 things that no amount of new construction can. It converts episodic, fearful spending into a predictable premium, so families seek care earlier. It gives providers a counterparty that pays on time, which lowers the risk premium on every rupee, rupiah, and peso they raise. And it creates a buyer with the scale to negotiate on price and the data to insist on quality. A payer that bargains is the only durable check on cost inflation in a market where the patient cannot.Penetration alone will not do it, and we should say so plainly.An insurer that pays out more in claims than it collects in premiums is not a payer; it is a subsidy with a delay. India's 4 public sector general insurers have run health claims ratios at or above 100% in most years of the past decade, against roughly 75 to 90% for their private peers, and that is before a rupee of operating cost. Public schemes carry a version of the same strain - tariffs set below the cost of care, settlements that arrive months late, and hospitals that quietly cap the beds they offer to scheme patients. The result is coverage on paper and rationing in practice. For industry to stay viable, public insurers must be run as underwriters rather than as instruments of policy, with tariffs that reflect cost, fraud controls that bite, and claims ratios that leave room to pay on time and still fund growth. A payer that cannot pay is no better for a family in Bihar than no payer at all.The objections are familiar - premiums are unaffordable, public budgets are strained, and private insurers cherry-pick. All true, and all solvable. Public schemes can anchor a floor of coverage for the poor while regulated private and employer products build the middle. Premiums can be collected through mobile wallets, payroll, and cooperatives, as they already are in Kenya and the Philippines. The actuarial pool improves the moment enrollment stops being voluntary. The technology to administer claims at scale, in local languages, with fraud controls, exists today at a fraction of what it cost in 2015. It is simply not yet used.The quieter fix, and the one that matters most over the long term, is digitization. Most Asian insurers underwrite in the dark. They lack longitudinal patient records, standard diagnosis and procedure codes, and claims data that can be read across providers, so they price on crude averages, reject on suspicion, and lose money on both. Claims ratios come down when health data becomes legible, and not before. India has the right architecture in the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission and the National Health Claims Exchange; adoption, not design, is the gap. Closing it takes a concerted effort rather than a pilot: regulators mandating standard codes and electronic claims, hospitals filing digital records as a condition of empanelment, and insurers pooling anonymized claims and outcomes data. At scale, this lets underwriters price by condition and geography rather than by age band, settle in days rather than months, and catch fraud before it is paid. Better underwriting is what makes premiums affordable over time, and affordability is what makes penetration stick.What is missing is sequencing, discipline, and a candid admission from those of us who deploy capital. We have been too comfortable investing behind the 20% or so of Asians who can already pay, and too quick to describe that as access. Access is measured by who comes through the door when they are sick, not by how many doors there are.Our plea is specific. Governments should treat insurance penetration as the primary healthcare metric, ahead of beds per thousand, and hold their own insurers to the claims discipline they expect of private ones. Regulators should let insurers, hospitals, and pharmacies share data and contract on outcomes, and should mandate the digital standards that make such sharing possible.And investors, one of us included, should put capital behind payers, third-party administrators, and the claims and data infrastructure that links them, with the same conviction we have shown for hospitals.Asia will add a billion people to its middle class this generation. Whether they arrive there healthy depends less on how many hospitals we build than on whether anyone other than the patient is paying when they walk in. The trap is well understood. The way out is too. It is time we financed it.
Article Summary: Summarize: Asia doesn't lack hospitals - it lacks payers. Insurance, not construction, breaks the out-of-pocket trap. WHO's South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions carry the highest share of people on Earth facing catastrophic health spending.

Article Title: Russia's diesel exports surge 100% after Trump lifts sanctions; not a single shipment reaches US
Article Text:
The US-bound shipments were diverted to other markets, including Brazil and Turkey

What was the Trump-Putin diesel deal?

Why deal sparked controversy?

Will Russia continue increasing diesel exports?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Russia nearly doubled its diesel exports in October after US President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase fuel supplies to global markets. However, none of the additional shipments has reached the US so far, with tankers originally headed for American buyers changing course amid opposition to the move and concerns over sanctions.Russia exported around 271,000 barrels of diesel per day in October, compared with 135,000 barrels per day in September, according to data provider Kpler. Instead of reaching the US, the additional Russian fuel went to markets such as Brazil and Turkey, allowing Moscow to increase sales despite uncertainty over the proposed American shipments, according to a report by The Financial Times.At least two tankers initially headed for the US have changed course in recent weeks. Another vessel carrying Russian diesel, the Agioi Fanendes, remains off the US East Coast awaiting a buyer. The White House said negotiations with the vessel's owner were continuing.The increase in exports came after Washington pressed Ukraine to pause attacks on Russian oil refineries and Trump announced an agreement with Putin on October 9.Trump announced the deal last month following a conversation with Putin, saying Russia had agreed to supply additional diesel to the US and global markets to bring down fuel prices.In a social media post, Trump had said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes after that. He also said Russia would deliver another three million tonnes within a short period.The announcement came as diesel prices in the US were rising sharply, putting pressure on consumers and businesses that depend on the fuel for transport, agriculture and other operations. High fuel prices were also a political concern for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.To facilitate the proposed supplies, the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License No. 135 on October 9. The licence temporarily authorised transactions involving the sale, delivery and import of Russian diesel that would otherwise have been restricted under US sanctions. It was issued for six months, allowing such transactions through April 2027.A White House official told the Financial Times that additional Russian diesel entering global markets would help ease prices for American consumers, even if the fuel was not delivered directly to the US.“As the President has said, this is a deal for the world. This deal was made to add diesel supply to the global market — lowering prices for Americans and the world — which is exactly what will be done,” the official said, as quoted by FT.The diesel agreement came after efforts in the US Congress to increase economic pressure on Russia over its war in Ukraine. One major measure was the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed into law by Trump on September 18.The legislation provided for additional sanctions against Russia and tariffs on Russian goods, as well as duties on imports from major buyers of Russian oil and gas and countries facilitating sanctions evasion. However, on October 16, Trump issued an executive order waiving the application of these measures, citing national interests and the need to pursue a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. It allowed up to 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian oil.A separate legal challenge has been raised by New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill over the proposed diesel imports. In a letter dated November 2, she argued that the Treasury Department's October 9 licence conflicts with the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, passed by Congress in April 2022. That law prohibits imports of Russian energy products, including diesel.Sherrill argued that the 2022 law does not give the president or the Treasury Department blanket authority to waive the import prohibition through a licence. She also said the administration had not met the conditions required to lift the ban and warned port and terminal operators that accepting Russian diesel could expose them to civil and criminal penalties. “New Jersey will not stand by while Donald Trump supports Vladimir Putin at the expense of Americans,” she said.The recent rise in exports may not last. Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian refineries on October 30, following a two-week pause. Russia has also extended its diesel export ban until the end of January, although some exceptions will be allowed.Richard Bronze, head of geopolitics at consultancy Energy Aspects, said the increase in exports reflected Russian refineries' ability to raise production during the pause in Ukrainian attacks. “If we want to attribute it, it would be the US pressure and Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire,” he said.However, Bronze expects Russian diesel exports to be “very lacklustre” in the coming months, as quoted by FT. “Russian refinery operations remain under significant pressure. We expect them to remain constrained around 4mn b/d in the near term, with limited prospects for a meaningful recovery as attacks continue,” said Sumit Ritolia, an analyst at Kpler.
Article Summary: Russia exported 271,000 barrels of diesel per day in October, up from 135,000 in September. The increase came after Washington pressed Ukraine to pause attacks on Russian oil refineries and Trump announced an agreement with Putin on October 9. None of the additional shipments has reached the US so far, with tankers originally headed for American buyers changing course amid opposition to the move and concerns over sanctions.

Article Title: 3 Indian-origin CEOs in race to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia chief
Article Text:
The company has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What we know about Huang's resignation

Poll Vote & Share your view Should Nvidia focus on appointing an internal or external candidate for the CEO position? Internal candidate External candidate Both options are viable 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Three Indian-origin technology executives, Sanjay Mehrotra, Nikesh Arora and Thomas Kurian, are among the names emerging in discussions over who could succeed Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia after the chipmaker's co-founder stepped down with immediate effect on Thursday.Mehrotra, CEO of Micron Technology, Arora, who heads cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks, and Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, feature among the potential contenders as Nvidia begins looking for a permanent replacement for Huang, who led the company for more than three decades, as per multiple reports.Nvidia announced Huang's resignation amid mounting scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO, while the company said its board would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones has also been appointed as Nvidia's first-ever board chairman.According to Bloomberg, Nvidia has engaged an outside firm to identify potential candidates for the position. The search is expected to be challenging, given Huang's central role in transforming the company from a graphics chipmaker into one of the world's most valuable technology firms and a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence processors.Mehrotra brings decades of semiconductor industry experience to the discussion. He has led Micron through the industry's boom-and-bust cycles, with the company's shares rising more than 2,700% during his tenure, driven in part by surging demand for memory chips linked to AI infrastructure.Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018, overseeing its expansion in AI-powered cybersecurity. Before joining the company, he served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and spent a decade at Google.Kurian, meanwhile, heads Google Cloud, one of the major players in the global cloud computing and artificial intelligence market. His responsibilities span cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and AI services, giving him experience managing large-scale technology operations and relationships with major corporate customers.Other names in the succession discussion include Nvidia CFO Kress and vice-president Ian Buck, who helped develop CUDA, the software platform that made Nvidia's graphics processors central to modern AI computing. External possibilities include Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple's chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned with immediate effect following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence agencies of being a Chinese spy. The company has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while considering internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, apologised to his wife, children and employees, admitting he had been “unfaithful to my wife”. The allegations have triggered national security concerns and calls for investigations in the US. Nvidia has maintained that there is no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised.
Article Summary: Indian-origin technology executives Sanjay Mehrotra, Nikesh Arora and Thomas Kurian are among the names emerging in discussions over who could succeed Jensen Huang. Nvidia announced Huang's resignation amid mounting scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO, while the board will consider both internal and external candidates.

Article Title: Anthropic IPO six times oversubscribed as AI firm targets record $1.4 trillion valuation
Article Text:
Anthropic IPO has already been oversubscribed

Revenue growth supports valuation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic’s upcoming initial public offering (IPO) has attracted orders for about six times the number of shares available, signalling strong investor appetite for what could become the biggest stock market listing in history.The strong demand for shares in the maker of the Claude artificial intelligence (AI) models could leave some prospective investors with smaller allocations than expected. Bankers have told investors that the company plans to prioritise existing backers, according to a Bloomberg News report citing people familiar with the matter.The reported level of demand and other details of the offering could still change.The company and some of its existing shareholders are seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion through the IPO, while a separate private placement is expected to bring in another $26 billion. Together, the two transactions could raise around $90.4 billion, potentially making it the largest fundraising exercise of its kind.Anthropic is offering 825 million shares at a proposed price range of $70 to $78 apiece. Its shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT.The company is targeting a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion.The IPO demand comes even as the AI industry faces questions over its dependence on advanced chips and the enormous spending required to develop and run AI models.Nvidia, a key strategic partner of Anthropic, has agreed to purchase about $10 billion worth of shares as part of the $26 billion private placement. Other technology companies participating in the placement include Google, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom, Micron and TSMC, according to the company's filing.Anthropic has committed tens of billions of dollars towards securing access to advanced computing infrastructure, including chips needed to train and operate its AI models.Anthropic’s rapid revenue growth is a key factor underpinning its ambitious valuation. The company reported a revenue run rate of $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, according to its filing.The figure stood at $65 billion at the end of July, Bloomberg News had earlier reported. The company calculates its revenue run rate by annualising consumption-based fees over a 28-day period and subscription fees for a single month.Anthropic has also stepped up efforts to attract investors ahead of the listing. Its chief executive officer, Dario Amodei, is scheduled to take part in a live-streamed event with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday.Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the IPO, with 20 other banks participating in the offering.
Article Summary: Anthropic is offering 825 million shares at a proposed price range of $70 to $78 apiece. Its shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT. The company is targeting a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion.

Article Title: Oil prices set for second weekly fall as Trump hardens stance on Iran, keeps military option open
Article Text:
Brent crude was trading at $95.41 a barrel, while WTI stood at $88.52, with both benchmarks on track for a second consecutive weekly decline.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Oil prices were largely steady on Friday but remained on track for a second consecutive weekly decline, extending a retreat from recent highs as expectations of a prolonged US blockade on Iran eased fears of an immediate escalation in the conflict. However, fresh threats from President Donald Trump and attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure continued to pose risks to Middle East supplies.Brent crude futures were little changed at $95.41 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell 20 cents, or 0.25 per cent, to $88.52 at 0242 GMT, reported Reuters.Brent was headed for a 2.4 per cent weekly decline, following a 16% plunge the previous week. WTI was set to fall 2.5 per cent, after losing 13 per cent last week.Oil prices had tumbled earlier this month after Trump played down the possibility of renewed strikes on Iran, with Brent settling at its lowest level since late August on November 9. Prices subsequently recovered over the next two sessions as attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and oil tankers heightened concerns over supply disruptions.The latest decline came after Trump said the United States did not need a deal with Iran to end the conflict, indicating that Washington would maintain its blockade on Iranian oil shipments, trade and economic activity.In a separate interview with Salem News Channel on Thursday, Trump issued a fresh warning to Tehran over alleged threats against American officials, saying those responsible for an attack on US officials "will not exist any longer".Read more: Trump warns Iran against targeting US officials Asked whether he would hesitate to use military force to stop Iran from threatening US allies and ships, Trump replied: "No hesitation." He also said further military action was possible immediately if the situation warranted it.The remarks underline the uncertainty surrounding the conflict even as crude prices have retreated from recent highs. Trump also claimed that the US had complete control over the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil exports from major Middle Eastern producers.Shipping risks remain elevated. Iran's military said on Thursday that four oil tankers had been hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the account.Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group also claimed to have attacked a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, an oil facility in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh.Adding to downward pressure on prices, US crude inventories rose by 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million barrels in the week ended November 6, according to the Energy Information Administration. The increase was significantly higher than analysts' expectations of a 1.1-million-barrel draw in a Reuters poll.Despite the decline, the threat of further attacks on tankers and energy infrastructure means the outlook for oil prices remains closely tied to developments in the Middle East.
Article Summary: Brent crude futures were little changed at $95.41 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell 20 cents, or 0.25 per cent, to $88.52 at 0242 GMT. Brent was headed for a 2.4 per cent weekly decline, following a 16% plunge the previous week.

Article Title: FBI seizes $1.2 billion in crypto stolen from Binance in record $6.3 billion heist
Article Text:
$6.3 billion were stolen form the world's largest crypto exchange last month

How did the $6.3 billion Binance heist happen?

How were the stolen funds tracked and frozen?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said Thursday that US authorities had seized or secured court authorisation to seize more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. The recovery forms part of a wider effort by US authorities and private-sector companies to track down funds taken in what is regarded as the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history.The October theft involved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets and has been attributed by the FBI to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group. The US government and private-sector partners have so far managed to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency. The Justice Department said it had obtained court authorisation to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of those assets, reported AP.The latest action is part of Washington's efforts to disrupt North Korea's alleged use of cybercrime to generate funds for its government and illicit weapons programme. US authorities have repeatedly accused Pyongyang of using sophisticated cyberattacks to steal digital assets and evade international sanctions.The incident took place on October 29, when hackers drained approximately $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance wallets used to process transactions. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes, according to blockchain records analysed by cybersecurity firms.The precise method used to breach Binance's systems remains unclear. The exchange initially suspected that a laptop had been compromised but later said its investigation had uncovered additional points of breach.Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said the attackers had compromised Binance's transaction-signing infrastructure, which authorises transfers and allows funds to be moved out of wallets. In simple terms, the hackers may not have needed to steal the actual wallet keys but instead gained control over the system that authorised the release of funds.Binance had said its investigation was continuing, while its co-CEO Richard Teng assured users that losses would be covered through the company's Secure Asset Fund for Users and its own resources.After draining the wallets, the attackers attempted to move the cryptocurrency across different wallets and blockchains to avoid detection and prevent the funds from being frozen.A significant portion of the stolen assets was held in stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC. Unlike decentralised cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, stablecoins can be frozen remotely by their issuers, making it possible for companies to block suspicious transactions when alerted by investigators.Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said the attackers attempted to convert hundreds of millions of dollars in stablecoins into Ethereum to move the assets beyond the reach of issuers. The firm tracked $325 million in stablecoin conversions into approximately $285 million worth of Ethereum over nearly 20 minutes.However, cryptocurrency companies, investigators and law enforcement agencies began freezing funds within hours of the attack. Chainalysis said the first freezes began at around 5:14 pm Eastern Time on October 29.The US government and private-sector partners have since frozen more than $2.7 billion worth of the stolen assets. The latest court authorisation covers more than $1.2 billion. Such cases generally involve forfeiture proceedings, in which the government files a claim before a judge determines who has a legitimate right to the recovered assets.The FBI has attributed the Binance theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking group accused of targeting cryptocurrency exchanges, decentralised finance platforms and investors to generate funds for the regime.Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said its investigators strengthened the link after observing funds stolen from Binance being mixed with cryptocurrency taken in a separate attack on exchange Bitget, which had also been attributed to North Korean hackers.North Korea has repeatedly been accused by US authorities of carrying out cryptocurrency thefts to generate revenue for its government and circumvent international sanctions. The funds are alleged to help finance the country's weapons programmes, including its prohibited nuclear and ballistic missile activities.
Article Summary: The FBI has seized or secured court authorisation to seize more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen last month from Binance. The October theft involved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets and has been attributed by the FBI to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group. US authorities have repeatedly accused Pyongyang of using sophisticated cyberattacks to steal digital assets.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.
